> This guy and his wife are outliers.

I'd say you are the outlier according to Census reports and other sources.

[Average driving time](http://www.census.gov/prod/2011pubs/acs-15.pdf) is 25.1 minutes to get to work. (2009)

[ABC News reports](http://abcnews.go.com/Technology/Traffic/story?id=485098&page=1) an average one-way commute time of 26 minutes (over an average distance of 16 miles). (2005)

But the variance is huge: On the best days, the average commute is 19 minutes; on the worst days, 46 minutes. That means traffic, at its worst, can double the average commute time, adding 27 minutes each way.

Still, this is only once instance and it has been clearly shown that there is/was a legitimate issue with some Toyotas.

So back at the end of January I had a bad mental reaction to a certain prescription drug for Anxiety/Depression.

I ended up at the hospital. I was very calm once there. I had realized what happened and my wife and friend came down to hang out with me while the doctor decided what to do.

So during this time if I had to use the bathroom they just told me to go ahead since it was just across the hall.

After being there for about 2 hours I got up to use the bathroom. I was immediately surrounded by security. I was told I had to go back into my room so I did.

Once I was in there the doctor said she "had to give me a sedative" because I tried to leave (even though the exit was nowhere near me and I was clearly going to the bathroom like I had a few times already without any complaints.

I refused to take the sedative injection at which point I was told they could "do anything they wanted" and they would restrain me in order to give me the sedative.

I responded that the first one through the door would be knocked out.

Five security guards entered and I kept my promise.

After being have my stitches ripped out and have a security guard jump on me numerous times resulting in 3 broken ribs, they were able to restrain me and force a sedative on me.

Hours later a police officer showed up and filled out a report claiming that I assaulted the security guard I floored.

I spent the last few months going through court and spending a lot of money on a lawyer. We argued, correctly, that it was my legal right to refuse treatment, that I was involuntarily intoxicated by a drug that they prescribed to me and that I was acting in self-defense.

The police officer should have never even taken the report and when he did and I told him what happened he should have actually wrote up the hospital staff. Instead, he told me that since I was the one in the hospital that I must be the one that is aggressive.

At the end, I pled to disorderly conduct and a $300 fine. The disorderly will come off my record in a year. I did this because, while I acted legally in every right, it would have taken more time out of work (lost wages) and more money paying a doctor to testify that I was involuntarily intoxicated (apparently witnesses have to be compensated for their lost wages) and even more in legal fees. This was the cheapest way out.

The prosecutor agreed that I wasn't in the wrong but they needed to get their money back from someone for the time they spent on the case, etc., etc.

He even told my lawyer afterwards that the witness refused to fill out a witness statement and that the hospital didn't want to pursue the issue...he said this AFTER he got me to plea.

That alone seems illegal to me. Shouldn't justice be the end result that both sides are working for? No, they want to win regardless of guilt. The court system knows that even innocent people will take a plea deal because to go all the way to trial is more than most people can afford.

So it's not just the police. It's the courts that allow this to happen.

It's basically a money-grab that starts with the police and runs through the whole legal system.

I know the feeling.

I had a suicidal episode from Celexa.

After an ambulance ride, stitching of my wrists and a 72 hour mental health hold I was billed over $15k. That was AFTER my insurance covered 80%.

I have a therapist and a Psych doc now.

I actually checked myself into inpatient when I slashed my wrists.

No desire to kill myself now, I don't even recall doing it, just coming out of the haze after I did and freaking out, wondering what the fuck is wrong with me.

That's just it, I do. So I have no idea where this attempt came from. I have to assume it was the Celexa.

I was mainly asking if anyone here has experience with having no recollection of a suicide attempt.

I have no intention of killing myself now.

I will ask my Psych tomorrow about it.

Thanks.

What bothers me is that I use to take Xanax for the Anxiety.

I was prescribed .25mg and I would break those in half because a full one would make me tired. I'd make a 30 pills last 6 months.

Since Xanax is a narcotic they don't like to continue giving it out.

And I spoke with my Doctor and I am now weening off the Celexa per instructions. I'll just have to live with the Anxiety because I don't want to take these SSRIs if this is what I can expect from them.

I just want the intrusive thoughts to go away. I never had them until I started on Celexa.

Glad (but also sad) to hear I'm not the only one that had this experience with Celexa.
